utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-02-54-R77.5-PT, in the case against Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My name is Bruce MacFarlane. I'm an attorney from Canada and have been appointed as amicus curiae prosecutor in these proceedings. With me this morning, and throughout the proceedings, is Lori Ann Wanlin, to my right. She is also from Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. MacFarlane. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Representing Ms. Hartmann, who sits behind, is my co-counsel, Guenal Mettraux, our intern Samrina Mohamad, and myself, Karim Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Khan. I would like to confirm with you, Madam Hartmann, that you are receiving interpretation and can understand the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Should you encounter any difficulties in that regard at any time, please let us know. Now, pursuant to Rule 73 bis of the Rules, the purpose of this Pre-trial Conference is to determine the number of witnesses the Prosecution may call and the time that it may take to present its evidence. The Chamber notes the Prosecution's amended Rule 65 ter witness list filed last week on 11th of June, 2009, in which the Prosecution lists two witnesses, a Robin Vincent and Yorric Kermarrec, that it intends to call for a total of three hours. At the Status Conference on the 19th of May, the Prosecution indicated that it would require approximately four hours, which would include the tendering of documentary evidence and viva voce evidence. Has this estimate changed as a result of the removal of Mr. Ruxton from the witness list, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the situation has changed significantly. The case will be much narrower and more focused. There has been a reduction down to two witnesses. Each of those witnesses will be quite short, in terms of direct examination, probably in the vicinity of 10 to 15 minutes each, and as a result of the Bar table motion, which permitted the introduction of most, if not all, of the Prosecution's exhibits, that will no longer be required as part of the case. So my best estimate of the case for the Prosecution, including the opening comments and the tendering of the viva voce evidence, will be somewhere in the vicinity of an hour, an hour and a quarter, in that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. MacFarlane. Then the Chamber will determine that the Prosecution may have about one hour to one and a half hours for the presentation of its evidence. It is the understanding of the Chamber that the Defence currently seeks to call a possible five witnesses, for a total of 13 hours, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm glad to report that there has been a reduction to that anticipated schedule. I indicated, albeit only a few moments before Your Honours entered, to your senior legal officer that unless things change in an unexpected way, it is not my intention at this juncture to call my client to give evidence. There will be three witnesses for the Defence, Mr. Joinet, Nura Alispahic, and Natasa Kandic. Your Honour, the first witness, Mr. Joinet, we estimate his evidence-in-chief will be in the region of two and a half hours. The second witness, Nura Alispahic, will be 30 minutes, hopefully. And the third, Natasa Kandic, her evidence, we anticipate, will be heard on Wednesday. That will be in the region of two and a half hours. Your Honour, I don't know if that assists at all. As far as it may help Your Honours' planning, the anticipated cross-examination, and, of course, I don't bind myself at all until I hear the parameters and contours of the evidence led by my friend, but I don't anticipate that the cross-examination need be extraordinarily long. There is one caveat. One Robin Vincent, a lot of documents that I would intend to put to him and which could be quite time-consuming, in my submission, I can deal with by way of argument in closing speeches and also in the brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Can I cut you short, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The idea right now really is just to get the number of hours that the Defence intends to use. You've sort of given me something like seven and a half hours, and I would like to cut you down to six.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment there's five and a half hours for witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've given me two and a half for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Two and a half, two and a half, and 30 minutes. So, Your Honours, we will be under six hours, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Are there any other -- may the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The Chamber then would like to encourage the parties, to the extent possible, to prepare their questioning so as to elicit all public information from the witness first, followed by any confidential information, so as to minimise the need to go in and out of closed session. Okay? It reminds the parties again that the Chamber, composed of a Bench of professional judges, has no difficulty piercing through the evidence together, if it is presented in the manner as proposed. Okay? That concludes, on my side, on the side of the Chamber. Are there any issues that the parties would like to raise? Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have three points, one which I'll hold until the end, I would ask that we go into private session on. The first point is I wondered if the Chamber was in the position to provide any guide-lines to counsel on the length of closing address, and so that's the first point. The second point is, and I've raised this before the Chamber and I've raised it in writing with my learned friends on several occasions, at the moment I, as the Prosecutor, as opposing counsel, am listed on the Defence pre-trial brief as a Defence witness, and it seems to me that that's an extraordinary situation, and it strikes me that it would be useful to deal with that at the beginning because -- simply because it is truly extraordinary to have that occur. And I have a position on that, obviously, but I thought I'd raise that at this stage because it's -- it places me into a highly unusual situation, for opposing counsel to be listed as a Defence witness. The third point, I would prefer to move into private session. This won't take much more than about one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. As for closing arguments, having heard the parties' submissions on the time they're going to take and the number of witnesses, and I would imagine that the rest of my colleagues on the Bench would agree with me, I don't see any need for any more than 30 minutes per side for arguments, without closing briefs. As you finish, you just stand up and argue and we finish. Would that be okay? Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. From my standpoint, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Mr. Khan .

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, we have tried to be as efficient as possible in cutting down our time for this case. There are some subtleties in the defences being put forward. It is a novel area of law, in our submission. We will require, conservatively, but we hope to constrain ourselves to abide by it, an hour and a half for the closing speeches. Your Honour, given that the good name of our client is in issue, it is our submission that this -- and given the seriousness of the allegations, it is a modest request, in our submission, an hour and a half for a closing speech, on the facts of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, if it will help you, maybe you might file a written brief on that, but I think the Chamber would like to keep it at 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the principle -- I would vigorously ask, with the greatest of respect, that Your Honours give the most anxious scrutiny to counsels' assessment as to the needs, the demands of the case. Your Honour, there will be, with your leave, of course, a closing brief that will hopefully detail all the authorities that we will rely upon in support of the oral argument, and that, of course, would hopefully make the task of your deliberations easier, because, of course, after hearing the closing submissions in court, you'll have, as an aide-memoire, marshaled together all our written arguments. But it is our submission, and it is my very strong submission, that an hour and a half is needed on this case. It is not as straightforward as perhaps Your Honours, at this point, may think, and there are some subtleties that I think great expedition would result in the sacrifice in the fairness that my client requires to have this matter properly deliberated upon. Your Honours, in my submission, an hour and a half, an hour extra, is not too extravagant, and, of course, if I can cut it down, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, you started off by saying that the Bench must scrutinize your submissions. Now, we can't scrutinize your submissions unless we see them. You know, we've heard what you've just said now, and what you have just said, is what we can scrutinize, and nothing more than that. We'll give you, in consideration of what you've just said, an hour to present your argument, together with your written submissions, and I think that should be able to cover you. If you detail your written submissions in your final brief, and you can point us to the main issues in your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So be it. I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you like to change it to get an hour too, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm fine with 30 minutes. I just wanted to clarify one point. Was the Chamber directing that the written submissions be provided on the last day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. The Chamber was directing that there be no written submissions. But in the light of what Mr. Khan is saying, if parties would like to submit written submissions, of course, if they can be submitted on the last day, that would be very helpful, if that is possible. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's possible or not. I believe from my standpoint, it will be. I was just curious as to whether or not the Chamber had in mind certain time-frames so the matter proceeded with dispatch, in terms of written submissions and responses and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe if we could be of assistance in that respect. We could agree with the Prosecutor as to a date convenient to our colleague and with a view to make sure that the brief is filed before the closing argument. And if Mr. MacFarlane, for instance, would need a day or two or three prior to the closing argument, we'd be agreeable to file the brief, obviously with the leave of the Chamber, at any time after the closing arguments or before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is completely agreeable to you, Your Honour. We believe we would need no more than a couple of days after the end of the evidence to file a brief. If the colleague of the Prosecution needs more time, we are agreeable with that, we can agree with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then if the parties can come back to the Chamber with the agreed time-limits on that point. But one little point that we need to deal with is the word limit for those closing briefs. Do you have any indication, otherwise we have a limit that we can put.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, I think I have submissions to make, and I'm afraid that they would probably be in excess of those you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do I have in mind, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I believe it will be less than the 15.000 which the Defence would suggest would be necessary, Your Honour. The reason for that, as my colleague Mr. Khan mentioned, is the number of issues. And as Mr. Khan named them, subtleties, which we believe require some attention. But more than that, Your Honour, what we would wish to do with a view to assist the Chamber is to provide numerous authorities that we have located, identified, and for which we believe would be useful to Your Honours. We, therefore, believe that it would be most useful to have some generosity on the part of the Chamber in that respect. And as Mr. Khan mentioned as well earlier, we believe that this would be conducive to having a shorter rather than a longer closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be asking for 15.000?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That would be our submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So granted. Mr. MacFarlane, 15.000, no more than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Certainly no more than that. I'm a bit taken by surprise at the amount. I thought it would be considerably less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would have thought so too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: This is a contempt proceeding, the trial of which will last now a matter of days. The issues have been very thoroughly litigated throughout the course of the interlocutory proceedings. I'm -- it's my respectful submission that a submission of that length is not necessary. The issues are clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. MacFarlane. We'll keep it at 15.000. The entire 15.000 doesn't have to be used. You can give us 10 words, if you want to. Okay. Any other issue from your side, Mr. Khan? Nothing. That be the case, we can move straight into openings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: at 9.28 a.m. to be followed by the trial.
